name: Champa
summary: Cham kingdoms of central and southern Vietnam, a Hindu–Buddhist trading power for more than a thousand years. It left the brick towers of Mỹ Sơn.

knownFor.label: Mỹ Sơn temple towers
knownFor.note: Brick Hindu temple towers, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

knownFor.label: Champa rice
knownFor.note: A fast-ripening, drought-resistant rice taken to Song China, where it boosted harvests.

knownFor.label: Cham sandstone sculpture
knownFor.note: Hindu and Buddhist sculpture, now in the Museum of Cham Sculpture in Đà Nẵng.

knownFor.label: Đông Yên Châu inscription
knownFor.note: The oldest known literature in a native Southeast Asian language.

location.value: The central and southern coast of Vietnam, from about Huế down to Phan Rang.
location.source: Wikipedia: Champa (checked 6 Nov 2026); Hardy et al. (eds), Champa and the Archaeology of Mỹ Sơn (2009)

terrain.value: Narrow coastal plains between the Truong Son mountains and the South China Sea, with good harbours.
terrain.source: Hardy et al. (eds), Champa and the Archaeology of Mỹ Sơn (2009)

climate.value: Tropical monsoon with typhoons that strike the coast each autumn.
climate.source: Hardy et al. (eds), Champa and the Archaeology of Mỹ Sơn (2009)

resources.source: Hardy et al. (eds), Champa and the Archaeology of Mỹ Sơn (2009)

disasters.value: Typhoons and floods along the coast.
disasters.source: Hardy et al. (eds), Champa and the Archaeology of Mỹ Sơn (2009)

population.value: About 2.5 million at its peak around 800 CE.
population.source: Wikipedia: Champa (checked 6 Nov 2026); Hardy et al. (eds), Champa and the Archaeology of Mỹ Sơn (2009)

urbanisation.value: Capitals moved over time: Kandapurpura, Simhapura, Indrapura, Vijaya and Panduranga.
urbanisation.source: Wikipedia: Champa (checked 6 Nov 2026); Hardy et al. (eds), Champa and the Archaeology of Mỹ Sơn (2009)

disease.source: Hardy et al. (eds), Champa and the Archaeology of Mỹ Sơn (2009)

migration.value: Cham refugees fled to Cambodia after Vietnamese conquests; many Cham live there today.
migration.source: Hardy et al. (eds), Champa and the Archaeology of Mỹ Sơn (2009)

economicBase.value: Trade networks linking the Indian Ocean and East Asia, plus rice farming.
economicBase.source: Wikipedia: Champa (checked 6 Nov 2026); Hardy et al. (eds), Champa and the Archaeology of Mỹ Sơn (2009)

tradeRoutes.value: A key stop on the maritime route between India and China until the 17th century.
tradeRoutes.source: Wikipedia: Champa (checked 6 Nov 2026); Hardy et al. (eds), Champa and the Archaeology of Mỹ Sơn (2009)

wealth.value: No estimate is possible for this period.
wealth.source: Hardy et al. (eds), Champa and the Archaeology of Mỹ Sơn (2009)

moneyAndTax.value: Little is known; trade used gold, silver and barter.
moneyAndTax.source: Hardy et al. (eds), Champa and the Archaeology of Mỹ Sơn (2009)

inequality.value: Royal and priestly elites; slaves were traded.
inequality.source: Hardy et al. (eds), Champa and the Archaeology of Mỹ Sơn (2009)

governmentType.value: Kings ruling city-states that sometimes united under one overlord.
governmentType.source: Wikipedia: Champa (checked 6 Nov 2026); Hardy et al. (eds), Champa and the Archaeology of Mỹ Sơn (2009)

keyRulers.value: Bhadravarman I, Indravarman II, Jaya Indravarman IV (sacked Angkor in 1177), Che Bong Nga (14th century).
keyRulers.source: Hardy et al. (eds), Champa and the Archaeology of Mỹ Sơn (2009)

succession.value: Hereditary, but power shifted between rival royal centres such as Indrapura, Vijaya and Panduranga.
succession.source: Hardy et al. (eds), Champa and the Archaeology of Mỹ Sơn (2009)

institutions.value: Kingship modelled on Indian ideas; temples as centres of power.
institutions.source: Hardy et al. (eds), Champa and the Archaeology of Mỹ Sơn (2009)

stability.value: Whether Champa was one kingdom or a federation of rival polities is debated.
stability.source: Wikipedia: Champa (checked 6 Nov 2026); Hardy et al. (eds), Champa and the Archaeology of Mỹ Sơn (2009)

eliteConflict.value: Rival centres competed for leadership of the Cham lands.
eliteConflict.source: Hardy et al. (eds), Champa and the Archaeology of Mỹ Sơn (2009)

armyAndTech.value: A navy of war boats and armies with war elephants.
armyAndTech.source: Hardy et al. (eds), Champa and the Archaeology of Mỹ Sơn (2009)

majorWars.value: Wars with the Khmer (sack of Angkor 1177) and Đại Việt; decisive defeat in 1471.
majorWars.source: Wikipedia: Champa (checked 6 Nov 2026); Hardy et al. (eds), Champa and the Archaeology of Mỹ Sơn (2009)

territoryChange.value: Lost the north to Đại Việt step by step; after 1471 only Panduranga in the south remained.
territoryChange.source: Wikipedia: Champa (checked 6 Nov 2026); Hardy et al. (eds), Champa and the Archaeology of Mỹ Sơn (2009)

alliancesRivals.value: Long rivalry with the Khmer Empire and Đại Việt; tribute missions to China.
alliancesRivals.source: Hardy et al. (eds), Champa and the Archaeology of Mỹ Sơn (2009)

inventions.value: Champa rice, a fast-ripening rice taken to Song China around 1012.
inventions.source: Hardy et al. (eds), Champa and the Archaeology of Mỹ Sơn (2009)

scienceEducation.value: The Đông Yên Châu inscription (c. 350) is the oldest known literature in a native Southeast Asian language.
scienceEducation.source: Wikipedia: Champa (checked 6 Nov 2026); Hardy et al. (eds), Champa and the Archaeology of Mỹ Sơn (2009)

openness.value: Open to Indian, Chinese, Malay and later Islamic influences.
openness.source: Hardy et al. (eds), Champa and the Archaeology of Mỹ Sơn (2009)

communicationTransport.value: A seafaring people: ships carried trade between China and Southeast Asia; river boats inland.

religion.value: Hinduism and Buddhism from the 5th century; Islam from the 16th century.
religion.source: Wikipedia: Champa (checked 6 Nov 2026); Hardy et al. (eds), Champa and the Archaeology of Mỹ Sơn (2009)

languageWriting.value: Old Cham (from about 350 CE), Old Malay as lingua franca, later Middle and Modern Cham.
languageWriting.source: Wikipedia: Champa (checked 6 Nov 2026); Hardy et al. (eds), Champa and the Archaeology of Mỹ Sơn (2009)

artsArchitecture.value: Brick temple towers at Mỹ Sơn (a UNESCO site) and sandstone sculpture.
artsArchitecture.source: Wikipedia: Champa (checked 6 Nov 2026); Hardy et al. (eds), Champa and the Archaeology of Mỹ Sơn (2009)

socialStructure.value: Kings, Brahmin priests, nobles, farmers, traders and slaves.
socialStructure.source: Hardy et al. (eds), Champa and the Archaeology of Mỹ Sơn (2009)

sharedIdentity.value: Cham identity, which survives among the Cham people of Vietnam and Cambodia.
sharedIdentity.source: Hardy et al. (eds), Champa and the Archaeology of Mỹ Sơn (2009)

dailyLife.value: Wooden stilt houses; rice, fish and coconut; brick temple towers in towns.

neighbours.value: Đại Việt to the north, the Khmer Empire to the west, and China and Java by sea.
neighbours.source: Hardy et al. (eds), Champa and the Archaeology of Mỹ Sơn (2009)

ideasReligions.value: Indian Hinduism and Buddhism, later Islam from Malay traders.
ideasReligions.source: Hardy et al. (eds), Champa and the Archaeology of Mỹ Sơn (2009)

colonisation.value: Annexed by the Nguyễn emperor Minh Mạng in 1832.
colonisation.source: Wikipedia: Champa (checked 6 Nov 2026); Hardy et al. (eds), Champa and the Archaeology of Mỹ Sơn (2009)

riseSignals.value: Founding of Cham polities in the 2nd–3rd centuries CE and growth of sea trade.
riseSignals.source: Wikipedia: Champa (checked 6 Nov 2026); Hardy et al. (eds), Champa and the Archaeology of Mỹ Sơn (2009)

peakPeriod.value: The 9th–10th centuries, when the Indrapura kings built Đồng Dương and Mỹ Sơn flourished.
peakPeriod.source: Wikipedia: Champa (checked 6 Nov 2026); Hardy et al. (eds), Champa and the Archaeology of Mỹ Sơn (2009)

declineSignals.value: Defeat by Đại Việt in 1471, which captured the capital Vijaya.
declineSignals.source: Wikipedia: Champa (checked 6 Nov 2026); Hardy et al. (eds), Champa and the Archaeology of Mỹ Sơn (2009)

outcome.value: The last Cham territory (Panduranga) was annexed by Vietnam in 1832.
outcome.source: Wikipedia: Champa (checked 6 Nov 2026); Hardy et al. (eds), Champa and the Archaeology of Mỹ Sơn (2009)

overallCertainty.value: Medium. Founding date and political unity are debated.
